description: Reference table for bond perception (3D geometry -> molecular graph) on tmQM metal complexes. Built because a 2026-10-04 literature sweep found NO published number for this task on tmQM or any transition-metal corpus.

protocol.ground_truth: tmQM_X{1,2,3}.BO.gz Wiberg bond orders (same atom indexing as the .xyz.gz geometries)
protocol.note: each baseline is scored on the bond subset it can address; the subset is named per row. No published tmQM bond-perception number exists to compare against (2026-10-04 literature sweep).

comparison_status: NO PUBLISHED BASELINE EXISTS. Published bond-perception numbers are all on organic molecules (RDKit DetermineBonds 95.3% exact-type on a fixed GEOM-DRUGS cohort; OpenBabel 64.4%) and are NOT comparable: different dataset, different chemistry. RDKit DetermineBonds cannot process transition metals at all. The tmQM paper (Balcells & Skjelstad, JCIM 2020, doi 10.1021/acs.jcim.0c01041) benchmarks DFT level-of-theory only and defines no structure task, so it shares no metric with this.
key_finding: Connectivity is easy; bond ORDER is what fails on metals. Where each method produces a molecule at all, it recovers the bond connectivity essentially perfectly (RDKit-stripped F1(exist)=1.000, OpenBabel 0.985) but assigns the wrong bond orders (F1(type) 0.358 and 0.539; exact-type 0.035 and 0.028). The organic SOTA pipeline additionally only produces anything for 31.9% of metal complexes.

honest_framing.measured: All four numbers per baseline are MEASURED on this host, 360 complexes, seed-0 sample, BO threshold 0.3.
honest_framing.scope_caveat: Each baseline is scored ONLY on the bond subset it can address, named in its row. rdkit_stripped is scored on non-metal bonds only (it removes the metal before running); openbabel is scored on all bonds. The two rows are therefore not directly comparable to each other.
honest_framing.protocol_choice: Ground truth bond EXISTENCE comes from tmQM's Wiberg BO >= 0.3; bond TYPE is the nearest of single(1.0)/double(2.0)/triple(3.0) by BO magnitude. A SMILES-derived ground truth would give exact orders but needs an atom-mapping step whose failures would be indistinguishable from perception failures. The threshold and the type-rounding are protocol choices, not facts about the chemistry.
honest_framing.sample: 360 complexes is a seed-0 sample, not the full 33,429-complex target-metal pool. Per-metal breakdown is not reported here.
honest_framing.not_claimed: These are NOT SOTA comparisons — no SOTA exists on this corpus. xyz2mol_tm (the published metal-capable method) is NOT included: it is not installed and could not be fetched in this session.

controlled_comparison_2026_10_04.why: The table previously held only classical perception, so nothing in the project could answer 'does the learned bond head earn its place?'. The question has a specific shape: OpenBabel already recovers bond EXISTENCE almost perfectly and its documented weak axis is bond TYPE (metal-donor orders). That is the only axis on which a learned head can justify itself.

protocol.why_that_scope: The CFM is trained on hydrogen-free clouds, so scoring it over all atoms would measure it out of distribution while the baselines kept the hydrogens. Restricting all three to the same non-hydrogen pair set is what makes the rows comparable.
protocol.sampling: 150 per metal, six target metals, seed 0
protocol.aggregation: per-complex metric then mean over complexes

controlled_comparison_2026_10_04.reading: MEASURED, the CFM does NOT beat OpenBabel on either axis at this training scale: existence F1 0.612 vs 0.977, type F1 0.280 vs 0.505. The burden of proof is therefore on the learned head, and the number that would discharge it is the TYPE column at production scale. rdkit_stripped's F1(exist) of 1.000 is on the 30.3% of complexes it can address at all — it is NOT comparable to the other two rows, which is why success_rate is printed beside every row.
caveats: The CFM here is a 4-epoch probe (n_train=256), NOT a production model; the production config is 20 epochs over ~946 clouds.

The CFM's own training-time numbers use a POOLED aggregation (bond_type_macro_f1_pooled) while this table averages per complex. The two agree on a single complex (pinned by molmetal/tests/test_cfm_bond_type_metric.py) but are not interchangeable across a cohort.

OpenBabel is a mature deterministic toolkit; the CFM is 4 epochs of gradient descent. The gap is expected and is not by itself evidence that the head is worthless — it is evidence that nothing yet shows it is worth anything.

corrections.old_value: two classical baselines, each on its own subset, no learned model
corrections.new_value: adds a controlled three-way comparison on one non-hydrogen scope
corrections.reason: A reference table with no learned-model row could not support any claim about the project's own bond head. Measured under one scope, the head currently loses to OpenBabel on both existence and type.

corrections.new_value: same-protocol 900-complex table: CFM macro-F1(type) 0.4723 vs OpenBabel 0.5051 (still behind); CFM wins F1(exist) 0.9961 vs 0.9771 and exact-type 0.0978 vs 0.0300
corrections.reason: the old pair differed in aggregation, model scale, and cohort simultaneously; re-scored under one protocol

production_scale_comparison_2026_10_11.why: PAPER_SCOPE.md quoted 'bond_type_f1 0.9194 vs OpenBabel 0.505' as Paper B's headline. That pairs two numbers that differ in THREE variables at once. The same checkpoint was therefore re-scored under the bench's own protocol so the comparison is like-for-like.

variables_that_differed_in_the_old_pairi.aggregation: trainer gate = POOLED over all scored pairs (train_cfm_yuelbond_wasserstein.py:5010); bench = per-complex F1 then mean (bench_tmqm_bond_perception.py:752). The trainer's own comment at :4996 says they are 'not interchangeable' and the field name carries the _pooled suffix for exactly that reason.
variables_that_differed_in_the_old_pairi.model_scale: trainer gate came from n_train=26715; the bench's CFM row on disk came from a probe at n_train=256, epoch 3.
variables_that_differed_in_the_old_pairi.cohort: trainer gate used its own 192-complex val split; bench samples 900 (150 x 6 metals).

production_checkpoint_rescored.protocol: identical to controlled_comparison_2026_10_04: 900 complexes, 150 per metal, non-hydrogen pair scope, BO threshold 0.3, per-complex aggregation

verdict.the_0.9194_figure_is_withdrawn: The same checkpoint scores macro_f1_type 0.4723 here and 0.9194 under the trainer's pooled gate. Nearly a factor of two. 0.9194 is a real number for its own protocol but must NOT be placed beside OpenBabel's 0.5051, which is per-complex averaged.
verdict.the_head_does_beat_OpenBabel_on_two_of_t: MEASURED at production scale, same 900 complexes: bond EXISTENCE F1 0.9961 vs 0.9771, and exact-type rate 0.0978 vs 0.0300 (3.3x). Both were losses at probe scale.
verdict.the_head_still_loses_on_macro_f1_type: 0.4723 vs 0.5051, i.e. 0.0328 BEHIND. This remains the honest-negative on the axis the bond head was supposed to win.
verdict.scale_effect_is_real_and_large: Same protocol, n_train 256 -> 26715: F1(exist) 0.6118 -> 0.9961, macro-F1(type) 0.2801 -> 0.4723, exact-type 0.0011 -> 0.0978. The earlier 'does not beat OpenBabel at this training scale' verdict was true at 256 and is now only partly true.

for_paper_b.cite: the 900-complex same-protocol table, including the macro_f1_type loss
for_paper_b.do_not_cite: 0.9194 as a comparison against OpenBabel 0.5051; it is a different aggregation on a different cohort
